passage: Ammi held out the spoon. "Bhindi, Zeenat?" Zeenat, two, clamped her lips and turned her face into the chair. "No." Across the mat, her cousin Dilnaz, four, crunched a piece loudly. "Mmm! Crispy!" Zeenat stared. Dilnaz took another and grinned, green bits on her chin. "More, Khala, please." Zeenat pointed at Dilnaz's plate. "That." "The same bhindi?" Ammi asked, smiling. Zeenat opened her mouth, chewed slowly, then held out her hand for more.

qa.q: What vegetable did Ammi offer Zeenat?
qa.a: Bhindi.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's long stare at Dilnaz suggest?
qa.a: Zeenat seems curious and less wary; watching Dilnaz enjoy the bhindi made the strange food look safe to try.

qa.q: What changed Zeenat's mind, and how could Ammi use that at the next meal?
qa.a: Seeing Dilnaz eat happily was the turning point, so Ammi could seat Zeenat beside a child enjoying a new food instead of pushing the spoon. 🙂

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel about being watched and copied?
qa.a: Dilnaz is simply enjoying the snack, but being copied may feel nice, like being the big cousin who shows the way.

grounding: A toddler refuses a food until an older cousin eats it happily, then tries it.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. At snack time Ojas (2) pushed away the steamed carrot sticks again: "No, no." I didn't press. Trisha sat beside him, dipped a stick in curd and crunched it, swinging her legs. "Yum!" Ojas watched her for a long moment, then licked one stick and bit the end. He ate three more, glancing at Trisha after each bite. Plan: seat Ojas next to Trisha when new foods come out this week, and tell his parents what helped. — Ms Lobo

qa.q: What food did Ojas push away at snack time?
qa.a: The steamed carrot sticks.

qa.q: What might Ojas's glance at Trisha after each bite suggest?
qa.a: Ojas seems to be checking that it is still okay; Trisha's happy crunching is reassuring about this new food.

qa.q: What choice did Ms Lobo make when Ojas refused, and why did it help?
qa.a: Ms Lobo didn't press, which left room for Ojas to watch Trisha and try the carrots without a fight.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha had pulled a face at the carrots?
qa.a: Ojas would probably have kept refusing, because Trisha's enjoyment was the cue Ojas was reading.

grounding: A daycare note records a toddler trying carrots only after watching another child eat them happily.

passage: Under the neem tree in Nani's courtyard sat a basket of jamun. Payal, almost three, poked one and pulled her finger back. Too dark, too squishy. Nani held one out; Payal hid behind the charpai. Then Vandana from next door skipped in, popped two into her mouth and stuck out a bright purple tongue. "Sweet!" Payal giggled. She crept out, took the smallest jamun, and bit it with her eyes squeezed shut. Then she stuck out her own purple tongue at Vandana.

qa.q: Where was the basket of jamun?
qa.a: Under the neem tree in Nani's courtyard.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling as she bit the jamun with her eyes squeezed shut?
qa.a: Payal was still a little nervous, but brave enough to try now that Vandana had enjoyed the fruit.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Payal, and what could Nani try with other new fruits?
qa.a: The turning point was Vandana eating happily and showing a purple tongue; Nani could invite Vandana over when offering Payal something new.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Payal's purple tongue at the end?
qa.a: To Vandana it probably feels like a shared joke and the start of a game, since Payal copied the tongue trick back.

grounding: A toddler in a village tries jamun only after a neighbour child eats it with delight.

passage:
"Asif Bhai, can you ask Abbu for the rolling bag? The blue one with wheels." Irawati dropped onto the sofa beside her brother.
"You said rolling bags were silly."
"That was before. Now twenty-two people in my class have it. Twenty-two!"
"So? Do you like it?"
Irawati paused. "It… rolls."
Asif grinned. "Wow. Strong review."
"If everyone bought it, it must be good. Twenty-two people can't all be wrong."
"Twenty-two people can all see the same advert."
"Bhai!" She hugged her old red backpack to her chest. "I just don't want to be the only one."
"Ah," Asif said, softer. "That's the real reason, na?"
Irawati picked at the zip and didn't answer.

qa.q: How many people in Irawati's class have the rolling bag?
qa.a: Twenty-two people.

qa.q: What does Irawati's pause before saying "It… rolls" suggest?
qa.a: Irawati doesn't really love the bag itself; the number of classmates who own it is what makes it feel right.

qa.q: Asif's question "Do you like it?" was a turning point. What could Irawati decide after answering it honestly?
qa.a: Irawati could decide whether the bag is worth asking for on its own, or talk openly about the fear of being the only one with a different bag.

qa.q: How does Asif see the reason behind Irawati's request by the end?
qa.a: Asif realises it is less about the bag and more about not wanting to stand out, so the teasing turns gentle.

grounding: A girl wants the bag most of her class has, mainly because so many people own it.

passage: My name is Francis, and last term I begged for a spinning-top battle set. Everyone in Class 5 had one. At break they crashed tops in a tin tray and shouted. I didn't even like it much. The tops were loud and my fingers hurt from pulling the string. But thirty kids can't all be wrong, I thought. Ankita, who sits next to me, didn't have one either. "I'd rather draw," she said. When Mum finally bought me a set, I played for two weeks. Now it's in my cupboard. Ankita still draws. I kind of wish I'd asked myself what I liked first.

qa.q: Where did the children crash their tops at break?
qa.a: In a tin tray.

qa.q: Why did Francis want the set even though pulling the string hurt?
qa.a: Francis thought that if thirty kids all had it, it had to be good, even without really enjoying it.

qa.q: Looking back, what does Francis wish had come first, and how could that help next time?
qa.a: Francis wishes they had asked what they liked before begging; next time, Francis could try a friend's set for a while before asking for one.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the whole trend from the next seat?
qa.a: Ankita seems calm about not having one and happy drawing, so the craze probably looks like something that will pass. 🙂

grounding: A child begs for a game set because the whole class has it, not because they enjoy it.

passage: Class 4 observation, Devika, age 9. Today Devika asked if she could 'please, please' get the scented gel pens by Monday. When I asked why, she said, 'Ma'am, the whole class has them. If everyone chose them, they must be the best pens.' I asked which colour she liked. She shrugged: 'Whichever the others have.' Later I saw her borrow a friend's pen, write one line, and hand it back without much interest. I did not lecture. At circle time I asked each child to share one thing they liked that nobody else did. Devika talked about her grandfather's fountain pen for five minutes, smiling. I will mention this to her mother. — Manjula Rao, class teacher

qa.q: Which pens did Devika want by Monday?
qa.a: The scented gel pens.

qa.q: What does Devika's shrug about the colour suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Devika doesn't care much about the pens themselves; the wish comes from everyone else having them.

qa.q: What did Manjula Rao choose to do instead of lecturing, and what did it bring out?
qa.a: Manjula Rao asked each child to share something only they liked, and Devika happily talked about the grandfather's fountain pen, a liking that was truly Devika's own.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother use this note when the pens come up at home?
qa.a: Devika's mother could ask what Devika really enjoys, like the fountain pen, instead of simply buying what the class has.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child wanting the pens the whole class has, with little liking of her own.

passage: The river below the old bridge in Kothapeta was brown and fast after the rains. Karthik's cousins were already climbing the rail, whooping, and dropping feet-first into the water one after another. "Asif, come on! Everyone's done it!" Asif looked down. The current pulled at a branch and swallowed it. His stomach turned over. But nobody else looked worried; they were laughing, shaking water from their hair on the bank. Maybe I'm just a coward, he thought. Karthik slapped his back. "It's nothing, yaar." Asif climbed over the rail, held his breath and jumped. The cold hit like a slap, and the current dragged him sideways for a long, frightening moment before he grabbed a root. On the bank, the others cheered. Asif didn't feel like cheering.

qa.q: What happened to the branch Asif watched in the river?
qa.a: The current pulled at it and swallowed it.

qa.q: Why did Asif doubt the fear felt on the bridge?
qa.a: Nobody else looked worried, so Asif decided the fear must mean being a coward rather than a real warning.

qa.q: Where was the turning point for Asif, and what could Asif have done there instead?
qa.a: The moment Asif's stomach turned at the current was the turning point; Asif could have trusted that feeling and stayed on the bank, saying the water looked too strong today.

qa.q: What might Karthik have missed while saying "It's nothing"?
qa.a: Caught up in the fun, Karthik probably missed Asif's fear and how strong the current was, because the group's laughter made it all look safe.

grounding: A teenager jumps into a swollen river because the group seems at ease, overriding a strong private unease.

passage: Early December in Utrecht, and the canal behind the school had frozen for the first time. By four o'clock half of Felix's year group was out on it, sliding, filming each other, shrieking. "It's solid," Aiko called from the middle. "Everyone's on it!" Felix stood on the bank in his heavy boots. The ice near the reeds looked grey, not white, and he had heard it tick. There had been only two nights of frost. Still, thirty people couldn't all be stupid, could they? Maybe he was the nervous one who always spoiled things. He stepped down. Halfway across, something cracked like a knuckle. Everyone froze, then laughed. Felix laughed too, too loudly, and walked very carefully back to the bank, heart hammering.

qa.q: How many nights of frost had there been?
qa.a: Only two nights of frost.

qa.q: What was going on in Felix's mind while standing on the bank?
qa.a: Felix noticed the grey ice and the ticking but told himself thirty people couldn't all be wrong, and worried about being the one who spoils things.

qa.q: Which moment could have gone differently for Felix, and how?
qa.a: Just before stepping down, Felix could have trusted the grey ice and the ticking sound and stayed on the bank, maybe calling the others off.

qa.q: How might Aiko see things after hearing the crack?
qa.a: Aiko, who had called the ice solid, might suddenly realise the group's confidence was just everyone copying each other, and feel shaken too. 😰

grounding: A teenager walks onto thin canal ice because the whole group seems comfortable, overriding his own doubts.

passage: At the district cricket academy, the new craze was batting against the bowling machine without a helmet. "Real batters read the ball," Akash said, cranking the speed dial up another notch. One by one the under-17 squad took their turn, bareheaded, grinning for the phone camera. Aparna unbuckled her helmet slowly. Her mother had saved for two months to buy it, and her fingers didn't want to let go. But everyone was laughing, even Rohini, who was usually careful. So maybe the fear was just her being soft. She set the helmet on the bench and took guard. The third ball reared off a crack in the mat and hissed past her ear. The nets went quiet. Aparna stayed at the crease, bat shaking, and pretended to grin.

qa.q: What was the new craze at the district cricket academy?
qa.a: Batting against the bowling machine without a helmet.

qa.q: What do Aparna's fingers holding on to the helmet suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Aparna's own judgment was saying no; the fear was real, even though the group's laughter made it seem silly.

qa.q: At what moment could Aparna have chosen differently, and what might that look like?
qa.a: While unbuckling the helmet, Aparna could have kept it on and batted anyway; one careful player makes it easier for others to do the same.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when the ball hissed past Aparna's ear?
qa.a: Akash, who kept turning up the speed, might suddenly feel scared and responsible, seeing that the challenge was dangerous rather than brave.

grounding: A teenager removes her helmet for a risky trend because the whole squad seems at ease, doubting her own fear.

passage: The Solapur bus stopped for twenty minutes at Mohol, and Hemant jumped down, starving. Two eateries faced the stand. One was packed, benches full, people standing with plates. The other was half empty, a man frying vadas in a clean kadhai. "That one," Hemant said, pointing at the crowd. "So many people can't be wrong." Omkar raised an eyebrow. "You didn't even look at the menu." "Don't need to." They squeezed in, waited twelve minutes, and got lukewarm poha. Hemant ate fast, watching the clock. Omkar glanced out. "That crowd is all from our bus. They just followed the first ones who got down." Across the road, the vada man was finally getting customers from another bus, and the vadas looked hot.

qa.q: What did Hemant and Omkar get after waiting?
qa.a: Lukewarm poha.

qa.q: What was Hemant thinking when pointing at the crowded eatery?
qa.a: Hemant assumed a packed place must be good, treating the number of people as proof of quality.

qa.q: What quick check could Hemant have made before choosing, with only twenty minutes to spare?
qa.a: Hemant could have glanced at both kitchens and menus, like the clean kadhai and fresh vadas, instead of trusting the crowd.

qa.q: How might the vada man across the road see busy stands like the other one?
qa.a: The vada man may know that travellers follow the first few people off a bus, so a clean, good stall can sit empty just because nobody went first.

grounding: A young adult picks the crowded eatery at a bus stop without checking, taking the crowd as proof of quality.

passage: Tomas had one evening to pick a summer course before the student discount ran out. He opened the course site, sorted by rating, and there it was: Data Analysis Essentials, 4.9 stars, twelve thousand reviews. He paid without opening the syllabus. "Twelve thousand people," he told Mateo across the tiny kitchen of their flat in Valencia. "It has to be good." Mateo, stirring rice, asked, "Good for who?" Tomas waved him off. Two weeks later he was watching a video on how to open a spreadsheet. The next module explained what a column was. Tomas had used spreadsheets at his part-time job for two years. He scrolled down to the reviews and read one properly for the first time: "Perfect for total beginners like me!"

qa.q: How many reviews did the course have?
qa.a: Twelve thousand reviews.

qa.q: Why did Tomas feel sure enough to pay without opening the syllabus?
qa.a: Tomas took the high star count and huge number of reviews as proof the course was good, so checking seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: What did Mateo's question "Good for who?" point to, and what could Tomas do differently next time?
qa.a: It pointed to fit: a course can be great for beginners and wrong for someone with experience. Next time Tomas could read a few reviews and the syllabus before paying.

qa.q: How might the reviewer who wrote "Perfect for total beginners" see the same course?
qa.a: For that reviewer the course was exactly right, so the stars were honest; they just described a different learner from Tomas.

grounding: A young man pays for the top-rated course by star count without checking whether it suits him.

passage: The registration hall at the college was noisy, one desk per elective. The queue for Film Studies snaked past the notice board; the Urban Ecology desk had three students and a tired professor. "Film Studies," Sahil said, joining the tail. "Look at that line. Everyone knows something." Dolma stopped at the ecology desk and picked up the course outline. "Did you read what Film Studies involves?" "Watching films, obviously." "It's four written critiques and a long end-term paper. You hate writing essays." Sahil shrugged. "Then why is everyone in the queue?" Dolma looked along the line. "Because the queue was long when they got here." Sahil stayed where he was anyway, shuffling forward with the crowd, the outline still unread.

qa.q: How many students were at the Urban Ecology desk?
qa.a: Three students.

qa.q: What did Sahil believe the long queue showed?
qa.a: Sahil assumed that so many people must know the course is good, so the queue itself felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Sahil check before reaching the front of the queue?
qa.a: Sahil could read the Film Studies outline, as Dolma did, and weigh the four critiques and long paper against a dislike of writing essays.

qa.q: How does Dolma see the queue differently from Sahil?
qa.a: Dolma sees the queue as people copying whoever was ahead of them, not as information about the course, so Dolma reads the outline instead.

grounding: A student joins the longest elective queue without reading the course, treating popularity as evidence of quality.

passage: The path sign at the lake in Slovenia said the waterfall trail was closed, but a steady stream of hikers was stepping around the tape. "Everyone's going," Vera said, tightening her pack. "Must be fine." Elif watched them. Most were glancing at the people ahead, not at the path. "Or they're all following the first group who ignored the sign," she said. "Does any of them actually know?" Vera groaned. "You're going to ask someone." "One person. Someone who isn't in the line." Elif walked back to the mountain hut. The warden, wiping a table, didn't look up at first. "Rockfall last week. The lower bridge is loose." Elif thanked him and came back. Vera was already unlacing her boots by the lake.

qa.q: Why was the trail unsafe, according to the warden?
qa.a: There was rockfall last week and the lower bridge is loose.

qa.q: What was Elif thinking while watching the hikers step around the tape?
qa.a: Elif suspected they were copying the first group rather than acting on real knowledge, since most were watching the people ahead, not the path. 🤔

qa.q: What did Elif choose to do instead of joining or arguing, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Elif asked one independent person, the hut warden, who actually knew the trail; that settled the question with real information in a few minutes.

qa.q: How might Vera feel about Elif's check by the end?
qa.a: Vera groaned at first but seems persuaded, choosing the lake instead, perhaps relieved not to have followed the crowd onto a loose bridge.

passage: By Wednesday, eleven people on the fourth floor had cancelled their December leave. "Appraisals," Ritwik whispered at the water cooler. "Word is, anyone who's away in December gets marked down." Avni's own leave was booked: her sister's wedding in Jaipur. She opened the leave portal, finger over Cancel. Then she paused. Who had actually heard this from someone who knew? Ritwik had it from Neelu, who had it from "the finance people." Nobody had seen a policy. Avni closed the portal and walked down to the HR desk. Kashish, who ran appraisals for the floor, laughed tiredly. "That's the third person today. Leave has nothing to do with ratings. It's in writing." Avni went back upstairs and posted the policy link in the floor group.

qa.q: How many people on the fourth floor had cancelled December leave by Wednesday?
qa.a: Eleven people.

qa.q: What was Avni thinking while the finger hovered over Cancel?
qa.a: Avni wondered whether anyone actually knew the rule or was just passing along what others said, since the chain led back to vague "finance people".

qa.q: Why was going to Kashish a better choice than asking more colleagues?
qa.a: Kashish ran appraisals and could point to the written policy, while more colleagues would only repeat the same rumour.

qa.q: What is it like for Kashish when the third person that day asks the same question?
qa.a: Kashish seems worn out, watching staff cancel plans over a baseless worry; Avni's post of the policy may finally bring some relief.

grounding: An employee questions whether colleagues cancelling leave know anything, checks with the appraisals lead, and finds no such rule.

passage:
Dear Parul,
Quick question, and I need your honest answer, not the polite one.
In the last month, nine people from my old college batch have signed up for the same six-month digital marketing certificate. Every week another one posts a photo of their welcome kit, and the comments are all "Me too!" and "Best decision!" I almost filled in the form last night.
Then I noticed something. Not one of them works in marketing. They joined because the others did. I can't tell if they know something or are just following each other.
You've hired marketing people for three years. Does this certificate actually matter when you look at a CV? I'll wait for your reply before paying anything.
Love,
Vasudha

qa.q: How many people from Vasudha's old batch have signed up for the certificate?
qa.a: Nine people from the old college batch.

qa.q: What worry sits behind Vasudha's question to Parul?
qa.a: Vasudha worries the rush is just people copying each other and doesn't want to pay for something only because it looks popular.

qa.q: Why is asking Parul a wise choice at this point?
qa.a: Parul has hired marketing people for three years and isn't part of the posting crowd, so Parul can say whether employers actually value the certificate.

qa.q: What would change for Vasudha if Parul replied that the certificate matters little in hiring?
qa.a: Vasudha could skip it without feeling left behind, knowing the crowd's excitement wasn't backed by real information.

grounding: A young adult pauses before joining a certificate trend and asks one experienced, independent person whether it really matters.

passage: Playground note, Friday (Class 3 teacher). Mehak (8) would not walk past the old banyan by the back gate today. She held my hand and asked if a lady in white really lives in it. On Monday she laughed when Sonali first told the story. By Wednesday, four more girls had 'heard it too,' and the lady now 'cries at lunchtime' and 'took a boy's shoe.' Today Mehak whispered, 'Everyone says so, Miss, so it must be real.' I didn't argue. We walked to the tree together, looked at the roots and a squirrel's nest, and counted who had actually seen anything: nobody. On Monday I will ask the class where each version of the story started.

qa.q: What did Mehak do when Sonali first told the story on Monday?
qa.a: Mehak laughed.

qa.q: Why had Mehak come to believe the story by Friday?
qa.a: Hearing it from more and more girls, each adding new details, made it feel true; Mehak said everyone says so, so it must be real.

qa.q: What did the teacher choose to do instead of arguing, and why might it work?
qa.a: The teacher walked Mehak to the tree and counted who had actually seen anything, letting Mehak notice that many retellings came from zero sightings.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel on Monday when the class traces where the story started?
qa.a: Sonali might feel surprised, and a little sheepish, to see how a small story grew so big once everyone kept retelling it.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today is Thursday and now I am scared of the tamarind tree. On Monday Swati said a ghost goat lives in it. I said goats can't be ghosts. On Tuesday Raju said he heard it bleat at night. On Wednesday, three kids said the watchman saw red eyes. Today at lunch EVERYONE was talking about it, even the Class 6 boys, and they said it chews the swings. The swings DO have marks. So maybe it's true?? So many people can't be making it up. I walked the long way round to the tap so I didn't have to pass it.
Tomorrow I'll ask Swati who told her first.

passage: Gargi had fetched water past the old peepal by the village pond a hundred times. Then, on the walk home from school, Neelam said her cousin had seen a lantern moving in its branches at night. The next day the milkman's son said the lantern floated. By Saturday, women at the hand pump were saying a spirit swung from the lowest branch and tugged at dupattas. Gargi's Dadi clicked her tongue, but even she walked a little faster past it. That evening Amma asked Gargi to bring water. Gargi stood at the door, pot on her hip, staring at the dark tree. "Everyone says it," she whispered. "Everyone." She waited until her brother could come along.

qa.q: Who said the lantern floated?
qa.a: The milkman's son.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling while standing at the door with the pot?
qa.a: Gargi was afraid of a tree that had never scared her before, because so many people now repeated the spirit story. 😟

qa.q: When Gargi hesitated at the door, what could Amma have done?
qa.a: Amma could ask who had actually seen anything and walk to the pond with Gargi, showing that the story grew by retelling, not by new sightings.

passage: Counsellor's log, 14 August. Jeevan (Class 10) came in at lunch, uneasy. He said a rumour has gone round that Mrs Rashmi Nair, the maths teacher, marks down anyone who takes outside tuition. He first heard it as a joke two weeks ago. Now, he said, 'Nobody even asks if it's true. People have changed tuitions because of it.' He has watched classmates repeat the same story with new 'proof' each time: a low mark here, a stern look there. He admitted he almost believes it himself, because he has heard it so often. We talked about where it started; he couldn't name anyone who knew. Next step: I will speak with the principal and with Mrs Nair today, and plan a class talk on how rumours grow.

qa.q: What was the rumour about Mrs Rashmi Nair?
qa.a: That she marks down anyone who takes outside tuition.

qa.q: What was Jeevan worried about on coming to the counsellor?
qa.a: Jeevan was uneasy that nobody questioned the rumour any more, and that even Jeevan was starting to believe it just from hearing it so often.

qa.q: What did the counsellor choose to do after listening, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: The counsellor planned to speak with the principal and Mrs Nair that day and hold a class talk, so the teacher could respond and students could see how repetition builds belief.

qa.q: What might this rumour be like for Mrs Nair?
qa.a: Mrs Nair may notice students treating her with suspicion and switching tuitions without knowing why, which could feel unfair and hurtful.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a student noticing a rumour about a teacher harden into accepted fact through repetition.

passage:
12 Nov
Weird day. Two weeks ago Sunaina said, just guessing, that Mr Pinto, the new geography teacher, 'probably' got thrown out of his last school. Today I heard it five times. On the bus it was 'he was fired.' In the canteen it was 'he was fired for shouting at a kid.' By last period, Rehan swore his cousin 'knows someone' from that school. Nobody said 'probably' any more. When Mr Pinto raised his voice over the fans, the whole row went silent and swapped looks, like he'd proved something.
I asked Sunaina if she remembered starting it. She went red. 'I didn't mean it like that.'
Now I don't know how to un-start it.
— Nandini

qa.q: How many times did Nandini hear the rumour today?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling on going red?
qa.a: Sunaina seemed embarrassed and perhaps guilty, realising a casual guess had turned into something everyone believed.

qa.q: Now that the source is clear, what could Nandini choose to do?
qa.a: Nandini could tell classmates the story began as a guess and ask a trusted teacher or counsellor for help, since Mr Pinto is being judged unfairly.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto experience the row going silent?
qa.a: Mr Pinto may sense the class is suddenly wary without knowing why, which could make a new job feel lonely and confusing.

grounding: A student's diary tracks a guess about a teacher turning into accepted fact as each retelling adds certainty.

passage: The message reached Pallavi four times before lunch: a blurry photo of a white van and the words WARNING, CHILD-LIFTERS IN THE DISTRICT, SHARE WITH ALL MOTHERS. First from the college group, then from her aunt, then from two neighbours in Nandgaon. By the fourth time, Pallavi's stomach was tight. Four different people couldn't be wrong. She forwarded it to the family group and to the self-help group her mother ran. Uday, her cousin, replied within a minute: "Which district? Which date? This photo has been going round for years." Pallavi's cheeks went hot. "So you'd rather wait till something happens?" she typed. "Some people just don't care about children." She put the phone face down till evening. Then her mother read out the police station's notice: the photo was old, the child-lifter claim false. Pallavi deleted her forward and typed to both groups, "Please don't pass this on."

qa.q: How many times did the message reach Pallavi before lunch?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Uday questioned the message?
qa.a: Pallavi felt embarrassed and defensive; the hot cheeks and sharp reply show Uday's doubt felt like not caring about children.

qa.q: What could Pallavi have done just before forwarding, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi could have paused to ask Uday's kind of questions, which district and which date, since four forwards are not four separate sources.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after being told some people don't care about children?
qa.a: Uday may feel hurt and unfairly judged for asking simple questions, and might hesitate to question the next scary forward.

grounding: A young woman forwards a child-lifter warning because she has seen it many times, and treats her cousin's doubts as uncaring.

passage: In the student flat in Porto, Emil's phone buzzed again. Same message, fourth sender: URGENT! If a call comes from an unknown foreign number, DO NOT ANSWER. Emil forwarded it to three groups and, for good measure, to Priscila across the table. She read it and snorted. "Picking up empties your account? How would that even work?" Emil felt a flash of irritation. "Fine, ignore it. Don't come to me when you're broke." "I'm just asking how—" "Everyone's warning each other, Priscila. You're the only one laughing." She stopped laughing. Later that night, Emil's bank sent every customer a notice: just answering a call cannot empty an account, and the forward was a hoax.

qa.a: Emil could have asked Priscila's question, how picking up could possibly empty an account, and looked for an official source before passing it on.

grounding: A young man forwards a scare message because many people sent it, and treats Priscila's simple question as careless.

passage: Girls' hostel, Block C, 10 p.m. Rajni had heard the voice note five times: a man's worried voice saying bird flu had reached the city and anyone eating chicken this week would fall seriously ill. Her roommate had played it. Two floor groups had it. Her mother had sent it twice. Rajni forwarded it to the hostel group with STOP THE MESS CHICKEN in capitals. Vishal, the student mess secretary from the boys' block, replied: "Is there a notice from the health department? The mess buys from an inspected supplier." Rajni typed fast. "Sure, wait for a notice. Very caring, Vishal." Six people liked her reply. Only one liked Vishal's. Rajni felt certain, and a little proud, as she switched off the light. The next morning, the warden posted in the group: there was no health department alert about chicken in the city.

qa.q: How might Vishal see getting only one like?
qa.a: Vishal may feel isolated and painted as uncaring for asking a reasonable question, and may be less willing to speak up next time.

"But fifty in one week here? The hospital, the paper, the councillor would all be talking about it, not just forwards." Jasleen Bua looked at her screen. "Then I'll send my sisters this old article." passage: So, Pranav, you want the salt story. Fine. Last year my Nani's building group decided ordinary iodised salt was, quote, 'slowly poisoning the family.'
